gloss: Users can only hold 7 (±2) items in working memory — nav items beyond this threshold create cognitive overload
Users scan in an F-shape — critical content and CTAs must land in the first two horizontal sweeps
Content above the fold receives disproportionate attention — value proposition and primary CTA must live here
CTAs must visually signal what they do and where they lead — ambiguous affordances break task flow
Every extra step or decision in a task flow adds cognitive load — friction compounds and causes drop-off
Elements close together are perceived as related — grouping drives content comprehension without labels
Elements that look alike are assumed to share function — inconsistent styling breaks perceived grouping
Whitespace is not empty space — it directs attention separates sections and reduces cognitive load
Visual elements (headers color type) should look the same across pages — inconsistency signals separate products
Features that do the same thing should look and behave the same — functional inconsistency breaks mental models
Missing content that users expect (e.g. products not appearing in a list) reads as a system error not a design choice
ARIA roles and attributes must match element behavior — mismatched ARIA breaks screen reader announcement entirely
Semantic HTML and correct ARIA labeling ensures assistive technology can interpret and announce content correctly
Users should always know where they are and how to get help — support access is part of system status not a footnote
Users increasingly expect to solve problems without contacting support — FAQ and self-help must be available to all user types
Users need persistent signals showing how to navigate to help — burying contact in L2 nav fails wayfinding
